lead: Above a certain power, silica stops being a passive pipe. The light itself drives two scattering processes. Stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS) sends a frequency-shifted copy of the signal backward. Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) sends one forward. Both steal power, so they cap what a link can carry. The same physics is used on purpose in Brillouin sensors and Raman amplifiers. Only a few universities teach this.
prereq: You need the loss coefficient α from Chapter 2.1 and scattering from Chapter 2.3: Rayleigh scattering is linear, this is not.

blocks.text: Rayleigh scattering is linear: double the input power and the scattered power doubles. Nonlinear scattering differs. Past a threshold the scattered wave is amplified by the signal itself and settles at a fixed share of the power.

In SBS the signal and the backward Stokes wave beat together, and their beat pattern drives an acoustic wave in the glass through electrostriction. That acoustic wave acts as a moving grating and reflects light backward. The reflected wave is shifted down by about 11 GHz at 1550 nm. The Brillouin gain band is narrow, tens of MHz, so a narrow-linewidth laser reaches threshold at a few milliwatts.

In SRS the signal scatters off vibrations of silica molecules. The scattered wave travels forward, shifted down by about 13 THz. Its gain band is tens of THz wide, so it draws power from many wavelengths at once. The threshold is far higher: hundreds of milliwatts.
Both effects switch on when the gain collected over the effective length, g·(P/A_eff)·L_eff, reaches a fixed factor G above unity: about 21 for Brillouin and about 16 for Raman.

blocks.where: P_th is the threshold power in W; G ≈ 21 for Brillouin and ≈ 16 for Raman; A_eff is the effective core area in m²; g is the gain coefficient in m/W; L_eff is the effective length in m.

blocks.text: L_eff is shorter than L because the signal fades along the span; only the near end is bright enough to drive the effect.

blocks.where: α is the attenuation coefficient in nepers per metre (divide dB/km by 4343) and L is the physical length in m. For a long span L_eff → 1/α.

blocks.text: At 1550 nm, 0.2 dB/km gives α ≈ 4.6×10⁻⁵ Np/m, so 1/α ≈ 22 km: an 80 km span behaves like 22 km. Broadening the laser beyond the narrow Brillouin band raises P_th; the Raman band is so wide that linewidth barely matters.

items: SBS caps power per WDM channel. The backward Stokes wave returns to the laser and adds noise. Cure: stay below P_th, or broaden the line beyond the gain band.
SRS moves power from short-wavelength channels to long-wavelength ones. Short-λ channels droop, long-λ channels gain; the limit is on total power.
Used on purpose: Brillouin sensors read strain and temperature from the frequency shift; a Raman amplifier pumps a signal with light about 13 THz above it. Unit 6 covers amplifiers.

figure.caption: A signal enters the span. Raman scattering sends a forward Stokes wave shifted down by about 13 THz; Brillouin scattering returns a backward Stokes wave shifted down by about 11 GHz.

spec.aria: A signal at 1550 nm enters a long silica fiber, a forward Stokes wave leaves shifted down by 13 terahertz from Raman scattering, and a dashed arrow returns a backward Stokes wave shifted down by 11 gigahertz from Brillouin scattering.

examples.question: A 1550 nm span has A_eff = 50 µm², g_B = 5×10⁻¹¹ m/W, g_R = 1×10⁻¹³ m/W, and L_eff = 20 km. (a) Find the Brillouin threshold. (b) Find the Raman threshold. (c) A WDM system runs 4 mW per channel. Comment.
steps: A_eff = 50 µm² = 50 × 10⁻¹² m²; L_eff = 20 km = 2 × 10⁴ m.
4 mW exceeds 1.05 mW, so each channel is above the Brillouin threshold. Eight channels total 32 mW, far below 400 mW.
examples.answer: P_th,B ≈ 1.05 mW and P_th,R ≈ 400 mW, so at 4 mW per channel the link is limited by SBS, not SRS.
examples.check:
A = 50e-12
gB = 5e-11
gR = 1e-13
Leff = 2e4
PB = 21 * A / (gB * Leff)
PR = 16 * A / (gR * Leff)
print(PB)
print(PR)

examples.question: Interpretation only: why does doubling the laser linewidth help a link that is Brillouin-limited?
steps: SBS gain exists only within tens of MHz around the 11 GHz shift.
A narrow line sits inside that band, so all the power pumps one acoustic wave.
Spreading the power over several GHz leaves only a small fraction inside the band.
The effective g_B falls, so P_th rises and the Stokes wave stops building up.
examples.answer: Broadening the line lowers the power density inside the narrow Brillouin band, which raises the SBS threshold.

traps: Putting physical length L where the formula needs L_eff. An 80 km span at 1550 nm behaves like about 22 km.
Swapping the two: Brillouin is backward, GHz shift, narrow band; Raman is forward, THz shift, wide band.
Converting A_eff wrongly. 50 µm² is 50 × 10⁻¹² m²; a slip to 50 × 10⁻⁶ m² makes P_th a million times too large.
Using G = 21 for Raman. It is ≈ 21 for Brillouin, ≈ 16 for Raman.
Saying SRS limits per-channel power. SRS limits total launched power across all channels.

quiz.q: Which scattering is backward and which is forward, and by how much is each shifted at 1550 nm?
quiz.a: Brillouin backward, about 11 GHz; Raman forward, about 13 THz.

quiz.q: Give the order of magnitude of the SBS and SRS thresholds at 1550 nm for a narrow-line laser.
quiz.a: A few milliwatts for SBS; hundreds of milliwatts for SRS.

quiz.q: Why does the threshold formula use L_eff instead of the physical length L?
quiz.a: The signal decays as e^(−αz), so only about the first 1/α of the span is strong enough to drive the effect; extra length adds almost nothing.

quiz.q: A span has A_eff = 80 µm², g_B = 5×10⁻¹¹ m/W and L_eff = 20 km. Find the Brillouin threshold.
Why does SBS limit power per channel while SRS limits total power?
quiz.a: The Brillouin band is tens of MHz, narrower than one channel, so each channel acts alone. The Raman band is tens of THz and covers every channel, so they pump one another.

quiz.q: Why does broadening the laser linewidth raise the SBS threshold but not the SRS threshold?
quiz.a: SBS gain exists only within tens of MHz, so a broad line puts little power in the band. The Raman band is tens of THz wide, so the line still lies inside it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Distributed Brillouin sensing turns a whole fiber into a strain and temperature sensor for bridges and pipelines. Raman amplification uses the same 13 THz shift to pump a signal with shorter-wavelength light. Both effects are why high-power WDM links need careful power management.
